title: Love was his meaning (ch. 86)
hookLine: after years of pondering she understands: love was his meaning
tomorrow: why would Julian call Jesus our mother?

lines: A PLATE WITH YOUR NAME ON IT.
THE ANSWER, IN THE LAST CHAPTER.
cards: A container in the fridge with your name on it in marker. Somebody made extra and saved you a plate. There's no note explaining why.
The plate is the explanation. Julian of Norwich spent years asking what her showings meant: the blood, the thorns, the hard questions she'd been left with.
In the last chapter of her book, the answer finally comes, and it's as plain as that plate.

teach.b: First, the question. From the time of the showings, Julian says, she often wanted to know what our Lord meant by them. Second, the wait.
Fifteen years after, and more, she writes, she was answered in her inward understanding. Third, the answer, which comes as a little set of questions. Would you learn your Lord's meaning in this?
In Grace Warrack's edition: "Love was His meaning." Who showed it to you? Love.
What did he show you? Love. Why did he show it?
For love. Hold on to that, she is told, and you'll know more of the same, and never anything else. Fourth, how far back it goes.

In that same chapter she says that before God made us, he loved us, and that this love has never slackened and never will. Notice what she doesn't do. She doesn't swap the hard parts for something sweeter.
She reads the blood and the thorns through that one word.
Here's one to tell a friend tonight: a book that opens on a crucifix in a darkened sickroom ends, in its last chapter, on the word love.

how: Catholics read Julian's last chapter as a key to her whole book; some quote its answer, love was his meaning, at the end of retreats and in times of grief.

games.q: what does “love was his meaning” mean?
o: Julian's answer: love is what all her showings meant
a love poem Julian copied out for a friend in Norwich
a vow of love that Julian made when she entered a cell

games.q: love was his meaning — tap the pairs.

s: Julian understood the meaning of her showings right away
she says the answer came fifteen years after, and more.
love was his meaning means God only shows pleasant things
she reads the blood and the thorns through that word, not instead of them.
she writes that before God made us, he loved us
chapter 86: a love that never slackened and never will.

games.q: your grandmother's last letter is mostly instructions about her garden. your cousin says it proves she cared more about tomatoes than people. what's the Julian-style way to read it?
o: read who wrote it, what it gives and why: it's love, in her language.
admit it's a to-do list she simply forgot to sign with love.
set it aside until you know for sure what she meant.
games.why: Julian answered who, what and why with one word, love, and read even the hard parts through it. a garden list can carry the same meaning.

practice: Pick up, or simply look at, one thing near you that someone made, chose or gave you: a mug, a jacket, a note, a plate. Hold it in view and ask Julian's question of it: what was the meaning here?
Let the answer be love, even if the giver was clumsy about it, and stay with that one object until the sit ends.

wordCard.voice: Love was his meaning. Julian's answer, years after the showings, to what every one of them meant.

orig.note: Latin for love, the Church's word for self-giving love, as in Deus caritas est, God is love (1 John 4:8). Julian herself wrote in English: love.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: love was his meaning, the same answer to who, and what, and why. Go gently.
